svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two authorization gates on a Compute Engine instance, IAM roles and OAuth access scopes, how they intersect, why access scopes do not apply to gRPC calls, the default VM configuration of a broad Editor role behind narrow scopes, and the recommended cloud-platform scope
svg.title: Attached service accounts: two gates in series, and the older one is transport-dependent
svg.text: Two authorization systems, both of which must agree. The advice on the older one is to switch it off.
A VM’s effective permission is the INTERSECTION of what the role grants and what the scope permits.
Gate 1 — IAM roles
The modern authorization system.
Attached to the service account.
Policy evaluation — everything from
the last fifteen posts.
Applies to gRPC: YES
Gate 2 — OAuth access scopes
The LEGACY method. Predates IAM.
Attached to the INSTANCE, per-VM,
persisting only for the life of the VM.
Default OAuth scopes for gcloud and
the client libraries.
Applies to gRPC: NO
The catch: a scope is not a boundary, because it depends on the protocol
The same operation, from the same VM, as the same service account, is subject to the scope over REST
and NOT over gRPC. Client libraries choose their transport, and that can change with a version.
So “we narrowed the scopes” is a control that holds for some calls, not others, and may stop
holding after a dependency upgrade. That is a default, not a security boundary.
And the default VM is configured backwards
Default SCOPES: read-only Cloud Storage, plus write for logging, monitoring, trace. Narrow. Cautious.
Default ROLE: the default service account may hold EDITOR on the whole project (#39).
So in an organisation created before 3 May 2024, the legacy gate is the only thing making that safe —
and it is the gate that skips gRPC, and the one Google tells you to open.
The best practice, and why the two changes must happen together
Set the cloud-platform scope — all Google Cloud services — and control access with IAM roles.
In other words: open the old gate completely and stop using it.
But do that on a default VM and you remove the only thing limiting an Editor grant.
Fix the ROLE first, then the scope. Neither change is wrong; the order is.
Debug order when a VM fails a call IAM says should work: API enabled → scope → role. Scopes have no effect at
all if the related API was never enabled, and that produces the least informative error of the three.
A control you did not choose is still load-bearing, and removing it is a decision — even when the
documentation recommends it.
